articles.title: Team captain Angela Stanford rues missed putts by Americans and slow greens at the Solheim Cup
articles.summary: For Team USA, this Solheim Cup might best be remembered for two extraordinary putts. Captain Angela Stanford wishes there were more of them.
articles.body:
DEN BOSCH, Netherlands — For Team USA, this Solheim Cup might best be remembered for two extraordinary putts.

Captain Angela Stanford wishes there were more of them.

"I think we just didn't make enough putts," Stanford said. "And if you listen to everything I've ever said, Europeans always putt better. I don't know why."

That strength on the greens led Europe to a 15-13 victory on Sunday after three days at Bernardus Golf.

Jennifer Kupcho stunned Europe fans with two huge putts — totaling 120 feet — on Nos. 17 and 18 late Saturday to snatch an unlikely point for the Americans from the last match of the day and tie the score at 8-8 after four sessions.

The team broke out a crate of Dutch beer on the bus to celebrate.

"Had to pull out some bottles for Jen," the team said on its official X account.

But despite that high, Stanford said her team didn't come to terms with the speed — or lack of it — of the greens at Bernardus Golf.

"Even when we showed up in July here, they were faster," she said, adding that she didn't think that recent rain — and heavy downpours on Sunday — were to blame.

Stanford shouldered the blame for not preparing her players better for the conditions.

"This is the one thing I am kicking myself is that I just didn't keep pushing, you know, we got to figure out how to hit our putts a little bit harder, which is really difficult ... to change the way you putt," she said.

It wasn't just quick greens the Americans missed.

The support in the Netherlands was also a factor, specifically the loud European fans hugely outnumbering and out-singing the Americans who made the trip across the Atlantic.

"Our Americans were there, but they weren't as rambunctious as ... we're used to," said one of Stanford's assistants, Paula Creamer.

"We are very momentum people and with our fans it's important that we can feed off and get that energy from them," she added.

They should have that support in two years at Valhalla Golf Club in Louisville, Ky.

"The good news is they can show back up in Kentucky in a couple of years and make it right," Stanford said.

What's not yet clear is whether Stanford will be leading the team there.

On the last green, shortly after the defeat, she wasn't immediately ready to commit to another edition.

"Well, we have a pretty good pipeline. There are a lot of captains in line on the American side, a lot of good ones coming," she said. "So, yeah, I think we have a lot lined up ready to go."

While the U.S. had plenty of reason to celebrate on Saturday night, Europe quickly washed away the American hopes en route to a 15-13 Solheim Cup victory on Sunday in the Netherlands.

articles.title: Encore: Packers meltdown again, lose Week 1 opener to Vikings
articles.summary: The Packers blew a 21-3 lead in Chicago in January. Their encore? Blowing a 22-10 lead in Minnesota to open the 2026 season.
articles.body:
The Green Bay Packers blew a 21-3 lead in Chicago in January, ending the 2025 season in gut-wrenching fashion. The encore for Matt LaFleur's team? Blowing a 22-10 second half lead by giving up 29 unanswered points to the Minnesota Vikings to open the 2026 regular season on Sunday at U.S. Bank Stadium in Minneapolis.

The Packers failed in the red zone and kicked a short field goal to go up 22-10 with 5:46 left in the third quarter. From there, the Vikings scored 29 straight points, including 22 points in the fourth quarter as the Packers collapsed in epic fashion once again.

Meltdowns are becoming more and more common in Green Bay . The offseason focus was on finishing. You get what you emphasize? Not for this team.

The Packers gave up double-digit leads in back-to-back games against the Bears to end the 2025 season and have now started the 2026 season following the exact same blueprint.

LaFleur's team led 19-10 at halftime and were in control for most of the first three quarters. But everything got away from the Packers during the final 20 minutes or so, and now Green Bay will limp into Week 2 with a demoralizing defeat and a 0-1 record.

Jordan Love battled Brian Flores and his relentless blitzes all afternoon, but the wheels came off late. He lost a fumble on a sack, setting up a short touchdown run, and he threw an interception on a deflected pass under pressure to set up Minnesota's final score.

The Packers out-gained the Vikings 419 to 239 but lost by 17 points. Green Bay finished with 12 penalties, including multiple defensive penalties on Minnesota's go-ahead drive in the fourth quarter.

The Packers will go to New York to play the 1-0 Jets next Sunday.

articles.title: Packers outscored 29-0 at end of Week 1 loss to Vikings | Instant analysis
articles.summary: Green Bay Packers again blow a second-half lead to lose their 2026 season opener 39-22 against the Minnesota Vikings.
articles.body:
MINNEAPOLIS – At the end of three quarters, the Green Bay Packers hadn't trailed. They had outplayed the Minnesota Vikings , doubling their yardage. There was only one question left unanswered.

The same question they couldn't answer all of 2025.

After spending an entire offseason hoping things would be different, the fourth quarter happened. And it was the same script that's become much too familiar in Titletown.

The Packers collapsed yet again, losing their 2026 opener 39-22 to the Vikings . It was their sixth straight loss dating to last season. In four of them, including this opener, the Packers held at least a 9-point lead in the second half.

Their biggest lead against the Vikings was 22-10 with 5 minutes, 9 seconds left in the third quarter. From that moment, they were outscored 29-0 through game's end.

After keeping offense afloat, Vikings pass rush finally gets to Jordan Love

Matt LaFleur raised some eyebrows during camp when he said Jordan Love is the best he's ever been around at adjusting protections before the snap, considering his last quarterback was you-know-who, but Love spent most of the game showing why he got such lofty praise. It just wasn't enough. Love is approaching a level where defenses blitz him at their peril. The Vikings, with defensive coordinator Brian Flores, is about as good as it gets with the blitz. Only until the end did Flores' scheme start overwhelming Love, who finished 21-of-42 passing for 387 yards, two touchdowns and an interception. No matter how many explosive plays Love hit on Flores' blitz, he kept bringing them, and eventually the Packers offensive line no longer could hold on. The Vikings finished with four sacks, all in the second half, and Love was hit 15 times. The turning point came when outside linebacker Andrew Van Ginkle sacked Love unblocked on third down, stripped the football and set up a short Vikings touchdown. No quarterback could endure that onslaught of pressure, including one who usually handles it better than anyone.

Packers' improvised offensive line might be worse than last year

Anyone who followed training camp could have seen Aaron Banks ' absence coming Week 1. After never consistently practicing because of knee tendinitis, Banks was inactive. His lack of camp reps gave the Packers ample opportunity to prepare for an opener without him, but the coaching staff decided to stray from what they'd followed most of the past month. Rookie Jager Burton got most of the starting left guard reps replacing Banks, but it was Donovan Jennings getting the start. Maybe Burton wouldn't have been better, a rookie starting in the blisteringly loud road stadium, but the Packers' offensive line was overpowered all game. The most-glaring example came early in the fourth quarter when LaFleur elected to take 3 points off the board, which would have given his team an 8-point lead, in favor of a fourth-and-1 attempt – but Love couldn't pick up the yard. The Packers run game was absent all game, though. Running backs MarShawn Lloyd and Chris Brooks combined for 66 yards on 20 carries. After a full offseason, one of the Packers' biggest issues from 2025 is still a big problem. The offensive line isn't good enough.

Packers defense can't overcome its own mistakes

The Packers' lack of rushing attack put a lot of stress on their defense, which trailed in time of possession all game and occasionally appeared gassed even in the first half. Even still, it was the defense's only undoing that was too much to overcome. On the Vikings' go-ahead touchdown drive in the fourth quarter, the Packers three times had chances to get off the field. On the first, Javon Bullard 's illegal-contact penalty erased a split sack shared between Edgerrin Cooper and Devonte Wyatt on third-and-11. On the next third down, rookie defensive tackle Chris McClellan hit Vikings quarterback Carson Wentz to force an incompletion, but he landed on Wentz for what is considered a roughing the passer in today's NFL. It appeared the Packers would make a final stand in the red zone after Evan Williams intercepted Wentz, but a defensive-holding penalty on safety Xavier McKinney renewed the Vikings' possession. They scored one play later on a 3-yard run from Aaron Jones and never trailed again. Those three plays are exactly how teams do not finish games.

Keisean Nixon 's versatility will become key in Jonathan Gannon's scheme

After a training camp full of questions, Keisean Nixon wasted no time providing answers. On his first snap, Nixon tackled Aaron Jones in the backfield for a 1-yard loss. On his second, he intercepted a lame-duck pass from Kyler Murray , setting up a field goal on the Packers' opening drive. He finished with five tackles, including one for loss. He also had a half-sack and two quarterback hits, including one that forced an incompletion on the first play of the second half. Nixon didn't pitch a shutout in coverage, but for what the Packers need him to be in their defense, he was plenty. His versatility was especially impactful. Nixon is a former slot corner moved to the perimeter, and defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon was willing to mix blitzes into Nixon's workload, and it paid off in a handful of important plays. His playmaking ability is why the Packers stood fast in the veteran being a starter in their defense.

Trey Smack gets lesson in margin of error in NFL debut

Trey Smack got a hard lesson in the thin margins between success and failure in the NFL. The sixth-round rookie draft pick's debut had its highlights, including a 59-yard field goal that opened scoring and might have been good from 70. Smack made all four of his field goal attempts, including the fourth-quarter field goal LaFleur elected to remove. But he also pushed an extra point wide right after the Packers' opening touchdown, and that lonely point made a big difference in the game. Most significantly, it probably enticed LaFleur to chase the fourth-down conversion in the early fourth quarter, because Smack's field goal would have given the Packers only an 8-point lead. With the extra point, that same field goal would have made it a two-possession game with a 9-point lead. It's a tough job, being a kicker. On a day Smack showed off his leg, he also saw how important it is to make the easy ones.

articles.title: Packers-Vikings Final Score: Green Bay collapses again in 39-22 loss
articles.summary: The Packers found yet another way to fall apart late in a game and now sit 0-1 and at the bottom of the NFC North.
articles.body:
Matt LaFleur talked during the offseason about his team needing to be better in closing down games. Whatever he did to try to make that happen didn't seem to work, at least not for the first week of the 2026 season.

The Green Bay Packers led the Minnesota Vikings 22-10 early in the third quarter. When the final buzzer sounded, Minnesota had scored 29 unanswered points, dominating the second half in a 39-22 come-from-behind victory. The Packers' offense, which had scored on each of the team's first three drives of the game, fell apart, led by its offensive line; the defense committed penalties on three straight would-be third down stops on the Vikings' go-ahead drive. The special teams gaveth — Trey Smack hit a 59-yard field goal early and Bo Melton had a 59-yard kickoff return — and tooketh away (Smack missed a PAT and the team allowed a 69-yard kickoff return).

Ultimately, the team that couldn't close out a game without Micah Parsons late last season couldn't do it without him to start 2026. To make matters worse, it happened against a backup quarterback, Carson Wentz , who came in for a concussed Kyler Murray in the first quarter.

Jordan Love 's good start was marred by back-to-back late fumbles, brought about by poor protection by his offensive line against Brian Flores' sellout blitzes, as well as by a late interception partly caused by the same. The running game was practically nonexistent, with the team gaining just 66 yards on the ground. And the performance on 3rd downs was abysmal — Green Bay 's offense went just 3-of-12, compared to Minnesota going 8-for-15, plus getting multiple conversions via penalty as well.

Love ended the day with his second-highest passing yardage total ever, going 21/42 for 387 yards and two scores to Christian Watson . But too much of that had to come late with the team bleeding out and trying to gather itself after Minnesota scored two touchdowns in less than two minutes.

The Packers will now have to lick their wounds for a few days before they head to New Jersey next week to play the 1-0 New York Jets .

Jonathan Gannon's defense got off to an incredible start with a pair of big plays from Keisean Nixon . He made a tackle for loss on an Aaron Jones run on the first play from scrimmage, then hauled in a prayer from Kyler Murray on the second. Gannon brought a six-man pressure, with linebackers Zaire Franklin and Edgerrin Cooper joining the rush, and Franklin came unblocked right into Kyler Murray's face to force the interception.

Trey Smack delivered the next Packers highlight, continuing his strong performance from the preseason. Green Bay's offense picked up one first down on a run by Chris Brooks , then was held to a stop at the very edge of field goal range. Smack stepped up for his first official NFL field goal attempt just ahead of midfield, and he drilled a perfect ball through the uprights from 59 yards out for the Packers' first points of the season.

Their next points came courtesy of Christian Watson. After a Vikings punt, Jordan Love hit Watson perfectly on a crossing route over the middle of the field and Watson turned on the jets, cruising up the left sideline. He picked up a big block from Matthew Golden — which was initially flagged, but eventually ruled legal — and cruised into the end zone for an 81-yard score. Smack pushed the PAT wide right, keeping the Packers' lead at 9-0.

The next Vikings drive saw Kyler Murray leave with an apparent concussion. He took a big hit from Javon Bullard and Lukas Van Ness while going to the ground on a scramble and remained down on the field for several minutes. Bullard was flagged on the play — arguably he made helmet-to-helmet contact, though it did not appear to be a late hit — and Carson Wentz came into the game in relief.

Wentz helped the Vikings work into field goal range, largely via the handoff, but missed a third-down throw to Jordan Addison to bring on Will Reichard to make the score 9-3.

After a 59-yard kickoff return by Bo Melton that set the Packers up at the Vikings' 40, the offense had to settle for another Smack field goal, this one from 43 yards out. The two teams traded punts for a while, with the Packers getting a sack from Lukas Van Ness to force the Vikings to kick out of their own end one. Skyy Moore 's return then set the Packers up at the Minnesota 36-yard line, but the offense went in reverse with the line getting beaten like a drum up front, leading to another Whelan punt.

This time, Minnesota drove the length of the field, even after a sack by Keisean Nixon and Jonathan Ford on the first play of the drive. An unnecessary roughness call on safety Evan Williams and a couple of third down conversions by Wentz set up the Vikings in Packers territory. From the 39, he got a free play with Van Ness jumping offsides, heaving a deep ball to Justin Jefferson , who shook rookie cornerback Brandon Cisse and hauled in a touchdown.

That left the Packers with 1:55 on the clock and three timeouts to try to expand upon their 12-10 lead before halftime. Jordan Love drove them down the field in chunks. First it was a 23-yarder to Tucker Kraft , then 10 yards to Bo Melton, then 32 to Watson to get to the 7-yard line with 30 seconds left. A 5-yard run by Chris Brooks set up Watson's second touchdown, which came off a brilliant play design where he motioned inside and faked an insert block, only to release to the corner of the end zone.

That sent the Packers into the half up 19-10 and set to receive the second-half kickoff, but they were unable to move the ball and had to settle for a punt. Minnesota did the same, setting up the Packers back inside their own 20.

Love went to work. He connected with Matthew Golden for a gain of 13 while under extreme duress, then converted a 3rd down to Jayden Reed before finding Jonnu Smith wide open for a big gain of 43 yards to get inside the 10-yard line. Another drive bogged down close to the goal line, though, and Smack hit a short field goal to make the score 22-10.

Minnesota responded quickly, however, with a 69-yard kickoff return from Myles Price . After getting one first down on the ground, Wentz found T.J. Hockenson open over the middle for a 16-yard touchdown, pulling the Vikings back to within five points.

Love converted a 2nd and 20 on the next series after a sack, hanging in the pocket and finding Matthew Golden again for a huge 43-yard gain to set the team up in field goal range. Another failed 3rd down led to a Smack field goal attempt, but the Vikings were flagged for a penalty and the Packers preferred to keep the offense on the field on 4th and 1 instead.

Jordan Love tried a QB sneak, but a questionable spot ruled him just short of the line to gain, leaving the Packers without a score after having had the opportunity to take an 8-point lead. Wentz came out firing for Minnesota, finding Josh Oliver for 13 yards, but then Edgerrin Cooper came up with back-to-back sacks. Unfortunately, the second one, on third down, was wiped out by an illegal contact penalty on Javon Bullard, handing the Vikings a free first down. Shawn Hochuli's officiating crew made their presence known once again on an apparent third-down stop, flagging Chris McClellan for roughing the passer despite him bracing his body weight to ensure that it did not actually fall on Wentz.

Hochuli bailed out the Vikings a third time on third down inside the red zone. Evan Williams picked off Wentz in the end zone, but Xavier McKinney drew a holding penalty, and one play later Aaron Jones punched it over the goal line on a toss to the left, giving Minnesota the lead. The Vikings went for two and Jefferson caught the conversion, making the Vikings' lead 25-22 with 6:37 left to go.

The big story coming into the game was the Packers' offensive line. It became the big story at the end. With Brian Flores sending the house, MarShawn Lloyd took a loss of three then Love was sacked and fumbled on back-to-back plays. The second of those was recovered by Andrew Van Ginkel at the 1-yard line, and Jordan Mason ran in another touchdown one play later to suddenly turn a 5-point Packers lead into a 10-point deficit.

Two plays later, Love threw a tipped pass while under pressure and got picked off, effectively putting an end to the contest. It was all but official when Jefferson leapt to the pylon for his second touchdown of the day, putting Minnesota up 39-22. The rest was academic; Green Bay managed to drive into the red zone again but failed to find the end zone and ending the day with a shockingly disappointing result.

articles.title: The Good, Bad And Ugly From The Packers’ Collapse Against The Vikings
articles.summary: The Green Bay Packers blew another fourth quarter lead and fell to the Minnesota Vikings, 39-22, Sunday.
articles.body:
The Green Bay Packers experienced them time, and time, and time again in 2025. And eventually, it killed their season.

The Packers had to feel like they were in the same bad dream Sunday, when they blew a 12-point second half lead and suffered a 39-22 loss to host Minnesota in their season-opener.

The Packers led, 22-10, late in the third quarter, only to see the Vikings score 29 unanswered points. Minnesota outscored Green Bay , 22-0, in the fourth quarter alone.

In the Packers' 31-27 loss to Chicago in last year's wild card round, they were outscored, 25-6, in the fourth quarter.

Green Bay has now lost six games in a row dating back to last season and also hasn't won a game since Micah Parsons tore his ACL in Week 15, 2025.

Here's the good, bad and ugly from the Packers' season-opening loss, beginning with the Ugly.

SAME OLD, SAME OLD: Collapsing late in games was the story of the Packers' 2025 campaign.

Green Bay had double digit leads in the final minutes twice against Chicago and also vs. Cleveland and somehow went 0-3 in those games. The Packers' odds of losing all three of those contests were 1-in-250,000, yet they somehow did it.

That pattern continued Sunday when Minnesota scored 22 straight fourth quarter points in just 2 minutes 42 seconds and turned a 22-17 deficit into a 39-22 lead.

"I mean, we've just got to finish," Packers wide receiver Christian Watson said last week. "I think that's just got to be the mindset. When we get into that third and fourth quarter, regardless of being up or down, we've got to approach it like we're at 0-0.

"And I mean, I think it'll just come down to execution. We've got to find a way to execute in those moments. Regardless of the mentality, the mindset, it's just about doing it. We've just got to find a way to do it."

The Packers couldn't do it a year ago — and they couldn't do it again Sunday.

And until they figure out how to finish, they have no chance of success.

TRIPLE PLAY: Minnesota marched 83 yards to take a 25-22 lead with 6 ½ minutes left.

Three times on that drive the Packers appeared to have a stop. Three times, though, Green Bay was called for a defensive penalty.

First, nickel back Javon Bullard was flagged for illegal contact, wiping out an Edgerrin Cooper sack that would have ended Minnesota's drive.

Next, Minnesota quarterback Carson Wentz threw incomplete on third-and-3. But Packers defensive tackle Chris McClellan was called for an extremely questionable roughing the passer.

Then, Green Bay safety Evan Williams intercepted Wentz in the endzone. But safety Xavier McKinney was called for defensive holding.

On the next play, former Packers running back Aaron Jones had a 3-yard touchdown run, then Wentz hit Justin Jefferson on the two-point conversion to give Minnesota a 25-22 lead. The Vikings only added to the lead from there.

NO DISCIPLINE: Granted, it's Week 1, so teams are still rusty.

But there's still no excuse for Green Bay having 12 penalties for 98 yards. The Packers had eight penalties for 70 yards in the first half alone.

• Nickel back Javon Bullard was called for a 15-yard unnecessary roughness penalty that knocked Minnesota quarterback Kyler Murray out of the game in the first quarter.

• Center Sean Rhyan was called for holding that helped kill a drive midway through the second quarter.

• Safety Evan Williams was penalized 15 yards for unnecessary roughness on Justin Jefferson.

OUTER BANKS: Packers left guard Aaron Banks , who missed much of the preseason with tendinitis in his knee, was inactive.

"I don't think anybody'smore frustrated than I am," Banks said last week. "But like that does it no justice, no good, right? To be frustrated and angry all the time doesn't do any good."

The Packers signed Banks to a four-year, $77 million deal in free agency in March, 2025 and have gotten almost nothing back on that investment.

Banks dealt with back, ankle and groin injuries in 2025. When he played, he was mediocre, at best.

Banks earned an overall grade of 53.5 from Pro Football Focus last season, which ranked 64th among 81 qualified offensive guards. His pass-blocking grade of 52.2 ranked 68th among 81 guards, and his run-blocking grade of 54.6 ranked 58 th .

With Banks sidelined, undrafted Donovan Jennings made his first career start and played in just his third NFL game.

RISKY BUSINESS : Trey Smack made a 40-yard field goal early in the fourth quarter to give Green Bay a 25-17 lead. Minnesota was off sides on the play, though, so the Packers accepted the penalty and took the points off the board.

On fourth-and-1, though, Jordan Love was stopped for no gain on a quarterback sneak. For some strange reason, the Packers didn't have a "pusher" behind Love to give him the extra shove he needed.

When Love fell short, Minnesota took over at its own 17-yard line, drove for the go-ahead score and never looked back.

GAME CHANGER: The Packers held a 22-10 lead with 5 minutes left in the third quarter after a 26-yard field goal by Trey Smack.

Minnesota's Myles Price returned the ensuing kickoff 68 yards to the Packers' 28-yard line. Six plays later, Vikings quarterback Carson Wentz hit tight end T.J. Hockenson with a 16-yard touchdown pass that pulled the Vikings within 22-17.

THIS AND THAT: Green Bay rookie cornerback Brandon Cisse has all the makings of a future star. Cisse found himself one-on-one, though, with Minnesota star receiver Justin Jefferson late in the first half. Jefferson won the battle, made a nifty adjustment on a deep ball and hauled in a 39-yard touchdown behind Cisse. … Daniel Whelan , who set the Packers' single-season franchise record with a 51.7-yard gross average last season, had a chance to uncork one early in the third quarter. Instead, Whelan had a dud that traveled just 22 yards. … The Packers ran the ball for just 66 yards on 21 carries, a 3.1 average.

CHRISTIAN WATSON: The Packers gave Watson a four-year, $110.5 million extension in June. On Sunday, Watson showed why.

Watson had five receptions for 131 yards and two touchdowns in the first half alone. He finished with six receptions for 147 yards and the two TDs.

"Obviously they gave me the opportunity to be here for longer (with the contract extension), so obviously I take pride in that," Watson said this week. "And obviously the amount of money that they paid me to continue to do what I'm doing, so I'm just grateful for the opportunity."

Watson certainly made the most of his opportunities Sunday.

His first catch of 2026 was a memorable one, as he turned a 20-yard reception into an 81-yard touchdown reception that gave Green Bay a 9-0 lead midway through the first quarter.

Watson came free on a crossing route, 20 yards downfield. Watson, who entered the NFL with 4.36-second speed in the 40-yard dash, quickly got to the left edge. Watson picked up a key block from fellow wideout Matthew Golden , turned the corner and outran the defense for an 81-yard TD.

Just before halftime, Watson had a 32-yard catch down to the Minnesota 7. Two plays later, quarterback Jordan Love ran a nifty play-action fake and Watson leaked out and caught a 2-yard touchdown pass that gave the Packers a 19-10 halftime lead.

JORDAN LOVE: Minnesota defensive coordinator Brian Flores blitzed an NFL-high 51.2% of the time last season. Flores brought extra rushers even more on Sunday, but Love hung tough against the pressure.

Despite being sacked four times, Love never blinked, threw for 387 yards and two touchdowns.

BO MELTON : It was quite a week for Melton, who was released Friday, immediately signed back to the practice squad and elevated to the active roster.

Melton then did what he always does — he made plays.

Melton had a 59-yard kickoff return that set up a Trey Smack field goal. He downed a punt at the Minnesota 4-yard line. And he had a 10-yard reception for a first down before leaving with cramps.

TREY SMACK: Packers rookie kicker Trey Smack made his first NFL field goal attempt a memorable one.

Smack drilled a 59-yarder to give Green Bay a 3-0 lead just 3 minutes into the game. That was the second-longest field goal in franchise history, behind only Lucas Havrisik 's 61-yarder in 2025.

Smack finished the day 3-for-3 on field goals, although he missed an extra points.

WELCOME BACK: Tight end Tucker Kraft , playing in his first game since suffering a torn ACL on Nov. 2025, had three catches for 65 yards.

Kraft signed a four-year, $75 million contract extension on Saturday. That average of $18.75 million made Kraft the NFL's third-highest paid tight end, behind only San Francisco 's George Kittle ($19.1) and Arizona 's Trey McBride ($19M).

THIS AND THAT: Linebacker Edgerrin Cooper had seven tackles, two tackles for loss and a sack. … Cornerback Keisean Nixon had an interception, two quarterback hits, a tackle for loss and ½-sack.

articles.title: Matt LaFleur shredded by Packers fans after team collapses vs Vikings
articles.summary: Matt LaFleur's decision to take points off the board in fourth quarter of eventual loss to Vikings is leaving Packers fans frustrated.
articles.body:
It's a new season for the Green Bay Packers but you couldn't tell based on what happened at U.S. Bank Stadium.

Matt LaFleur's Packers picked up right where they left off in blowing leads.

The Packers held a double-digit third-quarter lead, 22-10, against the Minnesota Vikings on Sunday, Sept. 13, as they controlled the game from the beginning. You wouldn't know by looking at the final score.

The Packers not only lost, but were blown out in a disastrous finish, losing 39-22, as the Vikings scored the game's final 29 points.

Packers fans saw all of this last year, most notably in the team's wild-card epic collapse against the Chicago Bears when they allowed 25 fourth-quarter points. The Vikings outscored the Packers, 22-0, in this fourth quarter.

While it was a combination of events again that led to this meltdown, a decision that LaFleur made to take points off the board with the Packers ahead 22-17 early in the fourth quarter set the stage for this new collapse.

Trey Smack made a field goal to put the Packers ahead 25-17 but LaFleur decided to take 5 yards after a Vikings penalty instead of taking the three points. The Packers then faced a 4th and 1. He called a quarterback sneak and Love was stopped.

The Vikings went down and scored on the next possession. The momentum had changed and soon Collapse No. 1 in 2026 was complete.

articles.title: Quick takeaways from Packers' 39-22 loss to Vikings: A game turned by the officials
articles.summary: The Packers lost in infuriating fashion as the Vikings, heavily aided by the officials, pulled off a comeback that had to be seen to be believed.
articles.body:
The Green Bay Packers suffered one of the most baffling defeats in recent team history in the season opener (and that's saying something), falling by a 39-22 final score to the Minnesota Vikings in a game they seemed to have full control of.

Here are some quick takeaways from Sunday's flabbergasting loss:

This was far from a perfect game by the Packers, but they had things under control until Shawn Hochuli and his crew took matters into their own hands.

Up by five, Green Bay "surrendered" one of the fakest touchdown drives you will ever see, as they looked to have gotten off the field on defense three separate times before phantom penalties gave Minnesota chance after chance, ending in a touchdown which gave them the lead.

The Packers will undoubtedly draw plenty of criticism for "blowing" a comfortable two-score lead, and the capitulation after that fateful drive was disappointing, but the fact is abysmal officiating completely flipped this game on its head and cost Green Bay a victory.

The offensive line concerns were justified

Perhaps the number one worry entering the season for the Packers was the offensive line and how it would hold up against the unbridled aggression of Brian Flores. The answer: not well.

It was feast or famine for Green Bay's offense all game, as Jordan Love was regularly forced to make magic with Minnesota defenders running right at him.

It is hard to know whether Jager Burton or Anthony Belton would have fared better than Donovan Jennings at left guard, and he was far from the only issue. Jordan Morgan had a rough debut at left tackle and generally the Packers O-line could not get everyone blocked.

Not every defense will present the types of issues the Vikings will, but this was an ominous start.

It feels harsh to even criticize the Packers for how they responded to the Vikings being handed the lead by the officials, but Matt LaFleur will certainly be unhappy with the collapse, and the accusations of not being able to "finish" will be levelled at his team once more.

There was plenty of time for Green Bay to overcome the adversity, and instead they crumbled. After finishing last season on an extremely bitter note, they once again lost a big lead against an NFC North rival.

Great performances that will be forgotten

Jordan Love's stat line will end up looking ugly, but he was having a terrific game before the officials intervened and winning the battle with Brian Flores despite the play of the O-line.

Christian Watson also showed why he was paid handsomely during the offseason, putting up 147 yards and two touchdowns, while Edgerrin Cooper was everywhere on defense. Those two things bode well for the rest of the season.
